fetched_contents.text: HIV Among Indigenous peoples: A Review of the Literature on HIV-Related Behaviour Since the Beginning of the Epidemic Abstract From the early days of the HIV epidemic, Indigenous peoples were identified as a population group that experiences social and economic determinants—including colonialism and racism—that increase exposure to HIV. There are now substantial disparities in HIV rates between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in some countries. We conducted a comprehensive literature review to assess the evidence on HIV-related behaviors and determinants in four countries—Australia, Canada, New Zealand and the United States—in which Indigenous peoples share important features of colonization and marginalization. We identified 107 articles over more than 20 years. The review highlights the determinants of HIV-related behaviors including domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use. Many of the factors associated with HIV risk also contribute to mistrust of health services, which in turn contributes to poor HIV and health outcomes among Indigenous peoples. Keywords: Indigenous peoples, HIV, Colonization Introduction Across the globe, the impact of HIV has been particularly pernicious among socially and economically marginalized groups, such as men who have sex with men (MSM), sex workers and people who inject drugs (PWID). From the early days of the HIV epidemic, Indigenous peoples in some countries were identified as a population group that also experiences social and economic determinants that increase exposure to HIV [1, 2]. However, the official response to this vulnerability has often been limited and ineffectual. As well, relatively little has been written about what is driving rising rates of HIV among Indigenous peoples and, more than three decades after HIV was first detected, it is clear that HIV has become a critical health issue for these historically oppressed populations [3]. Indigenous peoples have long-standing connections to their ancestral lands, dating back many generations and pre-dating colonization. Although cultural, linguistic, and geographic differences exist within and across Indigenous populations globally, to a large extent, colonialism, racism, social exclusion, and the repression of self-determination act as the determinants within which Indigenous health is constructed [4, 5]. The past decade has seen considerable emphasis on and recognition of the social determinants of health: the economic and social conditions that influence differences in health status. These include social exclusion, experiences in early life, education, stress, social support, employment factors, housing, addiction, food and transport. Marmot and colleagues work in this area has highlighted the vast individual and group level differences in health outcomes driven by disparities across these various determinants [6–8]—factors that are particularly relevant to Indigenous peoples. In some countries, research now clearly indicates a link between the distinct social inequities experienced by Indigenous peoples and higher rates of HIV than non-Indigenous peoples [9]. Similarly, disparities in the timing of diagnoses as well as treatment outcomes between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in the same country pose significant challenges for health services and government agencies as we enter the fourth decade of the HIV epidemic. This study focuses on four countries—Australia, New Zealand, Canada and the United States—where Indigenous peoples represent a statistical minority and where Indigenous peoples share a history of political and social marginalization that extends into health access and outcomes. We acknowledge that there are Indigenous peoples beyond these four countries who also experience similar aspects of poverty and alienation. However, our focus on these four countries was due largely to the common experience of colonization, displacement and neglect, which have contributed to health and social disparities between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples. In these countries, Indigenous peoples have higher mortality and morbidity as well as poorer health outcomes than their non-Indigenous peers [10, 11]. Colonization saw a dislocation from traditional lands and cultures among Indigenous peoples who had and continue to have strong links to land. This alienation from territory and domination by outsiders adversely affected physical, social and emotional wellbeing by suppressing traditional life and customs [12, 13]. Subsequent legal, political and social marginalization was often coupled with racial prejudice to produce a reality of poverty, underemployment and poor education [14]. Residential schools and “stolen generations” exacerbated displacement and loss of identity and were often associated with physical and sexual abuse that affected future generations [15, 16]. Table 1 presents contextual data on demographic characteristics and HIV prevalence between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples in the four study countries. Rates of poverty among Indigenous peoples in these countries are higher than among non-Indigenous people. For example, in the United States, about 28 % of Indigenous peoples lived in poverty in 2000 compared to 12 % of the total population [17]. Table 1. fetched_contents.text: Stigma and Racial/Ethnic HIV Disparities: Moving Toward Resilience . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2014 May 1. Published in final edited form as: Am Psychol. 2013 May-Jun;68(4):225–236. doi: 10.1037/a0032705 Abstract Prior research suggests that stigma plays a role in racial/ethnic health disparities. However, there is limited understanding about the mechanisms by which stigma contributes to HIV-related disparities in risk, incidence and screening, treatment, and survival and what can be done to reduce the impact of stigma on these disparities. We introduce the Stigma and HIV Disparities Model to describe how societal stigma related to race and ethnicity is associated with racial/ethnic HIV disparities via its manifestations at the structural level (e.g., residential segregation) as well as the individual level among perceivers (e.g., discrimination) and targets (e.g., internalized stigma). We then review evidence of these associations. Because racial/ethnic minorities at risk of and living with HIV often possess multiple stigmas (e.g., HIV-positive, substance use), we adopt an intersectionality framework and conceptualize interdependence among co-occurring stigmas. We further propose a resilience agenda and suggest that intervening on modifiable strength-based moderators of the association between societal stigma and disparities can reduce disparities. Strengthening economic and community empowerment and trust at the structural level, creating common ingroup identities and promoting contact with people living with HIV among perceivers at the individual level, and enhancing social support and adaptive coping among targets at the individual level can improve resilience to societal stigma and ultimately reduce racial/ethnic HIV disparities. Keywords: Stigma, Discrimination, Disparities, HIV/AIDS, Race/Ethnicity Stigma and Racial/Ethnic HIV Disparities: Moving Toward Resilience The National HIV/AIDS Strategy, coordinated by the White House Office of National AIDS Policy, notes that “HIV disproportionately affects the most vulnerable in our society—those Americans who have less access to prevention and treatment services” (p. ix) and that the reduction of stigma is a critical step toward decreasing HIV disparities and health inequities (The White House Office of National AIDS Policy, 2010). Moreover, accumulating research demonstrates that societal stigma associated with race and ethnicity contributes to general disparities in mental and physical health (Williams & Mohammed, 2009) and health care (Smedley, Stith, & Nelson, 2003). Yet, there is currently limited understanding of how stigma contributes to racial/ethnic HIV disparities and what can be done to reduce the impact of stigma to alleviate these disparities. To address these gaps, we propose and review support for the Stigma and HIV Disparities Model and propose a resilience agenda specifying strategies to reduce racial/ethnic HIV disparities resulting from societal stigma. Stigma and HIV Disparities Model The Stigma and HIV Disparities Model in Figure 1 identifies fundamental processes in the relationship between societal stigma and racial/ethnic HIV disparities, including risk, incidence and screening, treatment, and survival. Societal stigma is social devaluation and discrediting associated with a personal attribute, mark, or characteristic such as race, ethnicity, or sexual minority orientation (Goffman, 1963). Societal stigma related to race/ethnicity ultimately contributes to and maintains racial/ethnic HIV disparities through its manifestations at the structural and individual levels. Furthermore, as depicted by bi-directional arrows within the model, societal stigma is sustained through the co-occurrence of its manifestations (Link & Phelan, 2001). That is, structural and individual-level stigma manifestations reinforce differences in status, resources, and social and political influence in ways that reinforce and justify societal stigma. Although the Stigma and HIV Disparities Model focuses on basic psychosocial processes, it recognizes that social context can critically shape the degree to which and how societal stigma is manifested. Stigma Manifestations At the structural level, stigma manifestations include residential segregation, historical traumatic assaults, and medical mistrust. Residential segregation, an enduring legacy of institutional racism, is a fundamental cause of racial disparities in health (Williams & Collins, 2001). Similarly, a history of traumatic assaults including slavery, oppression, genocide, cultural destruction, displacement, and land loss, has left an enduring legacy on the health and psychological well-being of members of devalued groups, including Native Americans/Alaskan Natives (Walters, Beltran, Huh, & Evans-Campbell, 2011) and Blacks (Jones, Engelman, Turner, & Campbell, 2009). For example, historical traumatic assaults have disrupted traditional Native medicine services and customs (e.g., herbal and holistic alternative medicine) and led to historical trauma, a form of psychological injury experienced as depression, anxiety, anger, and avoidance (Whitbeck, Adams, Hoyt, & Chen, 2004). A history of unethical medical experimentation as well as contemporary discrimination within healthcare settings has resulted in mistrust of healthcare, medical providers, medical treatments, and the public health establishment among Black, Latino, and other communities (Corbie-Smith, Thomas, & St George, 2002). This mistrust can take on the form of “conspiracy beliefs” or beliefs about large-scale discrimination by the government (e.g., “The government is using AIDS as a way of killing off minority groups”; “HIV is a manmade virus”) (Bogart & Thornburn, 2005). At the individual level, societal stigma associated with race and ethnicity is manifested as stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination among perceivers (Dovidio et al., 2008). fetched_contents.text: Comparison of late HIV diagnosis as a marker of care for Aboriginal versus non-Aboriginal people living with HIV in Ontario Show available content in Abstract BACKGROUND: Studies have found that Aboriginal people living with HIV/AIDS (APHAs) are more likely than non-APHAs to receive suboptimal HIV care, yet achieve similar clinical outcomes with proper care. OBJECTIVE: To compare the proportions of individuals diagnosed late with HIV between APHAs and non-APHAs within the Ontario HIV Treatment Network Cohort Study (OCS). METHODS: The analysis included OCS participants who completed the baseline visit by November 2009. Two definitions of the outcome of late HIV diagnosis were used: the proportion of participants with an AIDS-defining illness (ADI) before or within three months of HIV diagnosis; and the proportion of participants with a CD4+ count <200 cells/mL at diagnosis. Logistic regression analysis was used to assess the association between Aboriginal ethnicity and late HIV diagnosis. RESULTS: APHAs were more likely to be female and have lower income, education and employment. No statistically significant differences were noted in the proportions receiving a late HIV diagnosis defined by ADI (Aboriginal 5.2% versus non-Aboriginal 6.3%; P=0.40). Multivariate logistic regression analysis revealed a significant association between Aboriginal ethnicity and late HIV diagnosis defined by CD4+ count after adjusting for age and HIV risk factor (OR 1.55; P=0.04). DISCUSSION: APHAs were more likely to have a CD4+ count <200 cells/mL at diagnosis but had similar clinical outcomes from late diagnosis when defined by ADI. However, differences may be underestimated due to recruitment limitations and selection bias. CONCLUSION: Additional work is needed to address the socioeconomic and health care needs of APHAs. Keywords: Aboriginal peoples, Access to care, Cohort study, HIV, HIV diagnosis, Quality of care ---------------------------------------- Despite increases in HIV research and advances in care and support programs in Canada, the Aboriginal population remains both over-represented in the Canadian HIV epidemic and under-represented in research. In 2006, 27.3% of positive HIV test reports were attributable to Aboriginal peoples in Canadian provinces and territories that reported ethnicity data for HIV testing. In these provinces and territories, Aboriginal peoples represent 6.0% of the total population; therefore, Aboriginal people are over-represented by approximately 4.6 times in the HIV epidemic in Canada (1). Studies have found that certain subpopulations of Aboriginal peoples have more HIV risk factors (2) and a higher incidence of seroconversion given these risk factors (3). In 2005, the proportion of new HIV diagnoses among Aboriginal peoples attributable to injection drug use (IDU) was 53%, while the proportion among all Canadians was 14% (1), suggesting that Aboriginal peoples have a different set of risk factors and that HIV-positive Aboriginal peoples represent a marginalized population with limited access to care and support services in Canada. Limited access to primary health care services among Aboriginal populations in Ontario has been reported based on higher hospital admission rates for conditions that could effectively be managed in an ambulatory care setting when compared with the general population (4). For example, in Ontario, individuals from Aboriginal communities, rural communities and remote communities have been found to be diagnosed with diabetes at a later stage, and to be more likely to visit an emergency department or be admitted to hospital for diabetes management than individuals from urban and non-Aboriginal communities (5). Such a finding may apply to the HIV field, such that Aboriginal people may similarly experience a trend of late diagnosis for HIV. The high concentration of Canadian Aboriginal peoples in rural areas may also contribute to their limited access to health care. In 2004, 21.1% of the Canadian population, but only 9.4% of Canadian physicians, were located in rural areas (6). Additional barriers to accessing health care among Aboriginal populations include perceived racism, differences in cultural beliefs and values, and a shortage of Aboriginal physicians (7). Nearly all of the Aboriginal people living with HIV/AIDS (APHAs) in Canada have either been directly subjected to or had a family member who was subjected to the residental school system. Accordingly, access to health care services and the trust placed in health care providers by Aboriginal peoples is profoundly impacted by historical factors and the repercussions of the residential school system (8). Late diagnosis of HIV has important consequences for clinical outcomes as well as on health care costs. For example, late diagnosis of HIV (CD4+ count <200 cells/mL) is associated with higher mortality despite earlier initiation of therapy (9,10). In Alberta, individuals diagnosed with HIV with a CD4+ count <200 cells/mL were found to incur medical care costs twice as high as those of patients diagnosed with a CD4+ count >200 cells/mL in the year following diagnosis. In addition, HIV-related hospital care costs were 15 times higher for those diagnosed late (11). Furthermore, earlier HIV diagnosis creates opportunities to reduce the risk of subsequent transmissions by offering earlier treatment and thorough behavioural modifications (12,13). Several studies have identified predictors of late HIV diagnosis. In a Texan cohort, female sex and illicit drug use were associated with a higher CD4+ count at diagnosis, potentially from perceived increased risk in this population (14). In other studies, heterosexual contact and an absense of reported risk factors were often associated with late HIV diagnosis (15–17). Indigenous peoples face a distinct constellation of social disadvantages compared with non-Indigenous populations, and these disadvantages are deeply structural, intersectional, and often compounded across multiple life domains. The evidence points to poverty, lower educational attainment, reduced employment opportunities, and housing insecurity as core disadvantages, while systemic discrimination and stigma operate as both drivers and consequences of poor health outcomes. Cultural and geographic barriers further compound access to HIV prevention and care.

Poverty and economic disadvantage are repeatedly highlighted as fundamental. The WHO fact sheet notes that Indigenous populations have lower life expectancy than non-Indigenous populations in rich and poor countries alike, and children born in low-income settings face worse outcomes [N2-R1]. In the Indigenous HIV review literature, colonization, racism, social exclusion, and repression of self-determination are described as the determinants within which Indigenous health is constructed, with poverty, underemployment, and poor education identified as direct outcomes of marginalization [N1-F1]. The evidence also explicitly notes that Indigenous peoples in the four study countries have higher poverty rates than non-Indigenous peers, including 28% of Indigenous peoples in the U.S. in 2000 compared to 12% of the total population [N1-F1]. This economic disadvantage is not incidental: it shapes access to food, housing, and basic services, and it is tied to poor HIV outcomes because “many of the factors associated with HIV risk also contribute to mistrust of health services, which in turn contributes to poor HIV and health outcomes among Indigenous peoples” [N1-F1].

Education and employment disadvantages are similarly central. The Indigenous review literature states that subsequent legal, political, and social marginalization was often coupled with racial prejudice to produce poverty, underemployment, and poor education [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that residential schools and “stolen generations” exacerbated displacement and loss of identity and were often associated with physical and sexual abuse that affected future generations [N1-F1]. These historical and ongoing disadvantages are part of why Indigenous populations have poorer health outcomes and are more vulnerable to HIV-related risk pathways.

Housing insecurity and geographic barriers are also a key disadvantage. The Indigenous review literature emphasizes that colonization disrupted traditional lands and cultures, and that this alienation from territory and domination by outsiders adversely affected physical, social, and emotional wellbeing by suppressing traditional life and customs [N1-F1]. Indigenous peoples are often concentrated in rural areas, where access to health care is limited. In the Ontario study on late HIV diagnosis, the authors note that Aboriginal peoples may experience late diagnosis because of limited access to health care, high concentrations in rural areas, and barriers such as perceived racism, cultural differences, and a shortage of Aboriginal physicians [N5-F3]. This geographic and cultural distance from services is not only a structural barrier but also a source of mistrust, which further delays care.

Systemic discrimination and stigma are central to health outcomes. The Indigenous review literature explicitly states that Indigenous peoples have been identified as a population group that experiences social and economic determinants—including colonialism and racism—that increase exposure to HIV [N1-F1]. The stigma and discrimination literature adds that a history of unethical medical experimentation and contemporary discrimination within healthcare settings has resulted in mistrust of healthcare, medical providers, medical treatments, and the public health establishment among Black, Latino, and other communities [N3-F2]. This mistrust is described as a major barrier to HIV prevention, care, and treatment adherence, particularly among Indigenous peoples [N3-R4]. The same source also explains that Indigenous people living with HIV face barriers through stigma and discrimination inhibiting access to supports including family, peers, and community resources [N3-R2]. The broader Stigma and HIV Disparities Model shows how societal stigma manifests through residential segregation, historical trauma, and mistrust, and how these structural and individual-level manifestations reinforce differences in status, resources, and social/political influence [N3-F2]. This means that stigma is not a separate factor but a mechanism through which poverty, education, employment, and housing disadvantages shape health outcomes.

Cultural and geographic barriers to HIV prevention and care are therefore part of a single structural system. The Ontario evidence notes that perceived racism, differences in cultural beliefs and values, and a shortage of Aboriginal physicians contribute to barriers to care [N5-F3]. In the Indigenous review literature, the authors describe how colonialism and racism have produced poverty, underemployment, poor education, and poor health outcomes, and how these conditions also contribute to mistrust of health services [N1-F1]. Together, these sources show that Indigenous peoples do not simply face HIV risk because of individual choices; they face a complex set of disadvantages that include economic deprivation, educational disadvantage, employment barriers, housing insecurity, geographic isolation, and stigma.

Overall, the evidence distinguishes Indigenous peoples from non-Indigenous populations by showing that the disadvantages are not isolated or minor. They are structural, persistent, and multilayered. Poverty, education, employment, and housing disadvantages are direct features of Indigenous disadvantage [N1-F1][N2-R1]. Systemic discrimination and stigma are both drivers of poor health outcomes and barriers to care [N3-F2][N5-F3]. Cultural and geographic barriers further compound access to HIV prevention and care [N1-F1][N5-F3]. This pattern supports the conclusion that Indigenous peoples are socially disadvantaged in ways that are qualitatively distinct from many non-Indigenous populations and that these disadvantages operate together to shape HIV risk and outcomes.

The HIV-related risk behaviors documented in Indigenous populations include inconsistent and low condom use, substance use, and high-risk sexual behaviors associated with injection drug use and other risk factors. These behaviors are not unique to Indigenous peoples, but the evidence suggests that they appear in Indigenous populations within a specific social context shaped by colonization, marginalization, and structural disadvantage, and that their expression may differ in ways that overlap with and diverge from non-Indigenous findings.

Specific risk behaviors documented in Indigenous populations are most clearly condom-related and substance-related. The Indigenous HIV review literature states that inconsistent and low condom use represents an immediate risk factor for HIV infection, which also leads to high rates of STIs in Indigenous populations [N1-R1]. It also notes that among AI/AN women, reported risk factors for HIV include 54% heterosexual contact and 46% injection drug use [N1-R5]. This indicates that Indigenous peoples are at risk through both sexual and injection-related pathways. The broader review literature also highlights that domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use are determinants of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1].

Sexual behavior is central. The evidence explicitly identifies heterosexual contact as a reported risk factor among Indigenous women [N1-R5]. The Indigenous review literature also notes that HIV-related behaviors are shaped by social determinants including domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use [N1-F1]. This means that sexual risk behaviors in Indigenous populations are not simply about individual choice; they are embedded in broader risk environments.

Substance use is another major documented risk behavior. The Indigenous review literature explicitly states that substance use is a determinant of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1]. The American Indian/Alaska Native youth study on substance use and sexual risk behaviors notes that the prevalence of behaviors putting AI/AN high school students at risk for teen pregnancy and STIs was examined [N1-R2]. The CDC-linked excerpt also states that studies among adolescents show an association between substance use and sexual risk behaviors, including ever having sex, having multiple sex partners, and other high-risk sexual behaviors [N4-R4]. For Indigenous populations, this association is reinforced by the fact that substance use is tied to injection drug use and other risk factors [N1-F1][N1-R5]. The evidence also notes that IV drug use is recognized as a risk factor in Native communities [N1-R4].

Condom use is explicitly documented as inconsistent and low in Indigenous populations. The Indigenous review literature states that inconsistent and low condom use is an immediate risk factor for HIV infection and contributes to high STI rates [N1-R1]. The non-Indigenous literature in the search set supports the general association between substance use and sexual risk behaviors, including condomless sex and other behaviors linked to STI testing [N4-R2]. However, the Indigenous evidence shows that these behaviors appear within a context of colonization, racism, social exclusion, and repression of self-determination [N1-F1], which means that the same sexual and substance-use risk patterns may be expressed differently because of structural disadvantage rather than being identical to non-Indigenous patterns.

The role of sexual behavior, substance use, and condom use is therefore interrelated. Sexual behavior, particularly heterosexual contact and multiple sexual partners, is documented as a reported risk factor in Indigenous women [N1-R5]. Substance use is a documented determinant of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1], and it is linked to injection drug use and other high-risk pathways [N1-R5]. Condom use is explicitly identified as inconsistent and low, which increases vulnerability to HIV and STIs [N1-R1]. The non-Indigenous literature confirms that substance use and sexual risk behaviors are associated, with condomless sex and peer influence on sex and injecting drug use also being contributing factors [N4-R3][N4-R4]. However, the Indigenous evidence adds that these behaviors are not merely behavioral; they are shaped by social determinants such as poverty, underemployment, poor education, and mistrust of health services [N1-F1][N5-F3].

In terms of overlap and difference, the behaviors overlap with non-Indigenous findings in the sense that condom use, substance use, and sexual risk behaviors are all commonly associated with HIV risk [N1-R1][N1-R5][N4-R4]. But they differ in the way they are explained and in the context in which they occur. For Indigenous populations, the evidence points to colonization, racism, social exclusion, and repression of self-determination as the broader determinants [N1-F1]. This means that the same behaviors may be more frequent, more persistent, or more resistant to change because of the structural conditions in which they emerge [N1-F1][N3-F2]. The evidence also suggests that Indigenous peoples may face additional barriers to prevention and care, including stigma, mistrust, and geographic isolation, which can affect both risk behaviors and care engagement [N3-R4][N5-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports a distinction: Indigenous peoples do not have a unique set of risk behaviors in the sense of behaviors that are entirely different from non-Indigenous populations, but they do have risk behaviors that appear in a distinct social and structural context. The behaviors are consistent with general HIV risk patterns, but they are amplified by colonization, marginalization, and structural disadvantage [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R5][N4-R4].

Cross-population comparisons of Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations are shaped by important structural and methodological differences, and these differences make comparisons difficult and potentially misleading. The evidence shows that data collection and sampling differ across populations, that measurement bias can distort comparisons, and that the strongest evidence is generally from studies with explicit attention to Indigenous populations, longitudinal cohort designs, and careful consideration of social determinants.

First, differences in data collection and sampling across populations are substantial. The Indigenous HIV review literature notes that Indigenous peoples are overrepresented in the HIV epidemic in Canada, yet they are underrepresented in research [N1-F1]. The Ontario study on late HIV diagnosis explicitly states that Aboriginal people are over-represented by approximately 4.6 times in the HIV epidemic in Canada, while they represent only 6.0% of the total population [N5-F3]. This overrepresentation indicates that Indigenous populations may not be sampled proportionally in many HIV datasets, which can distort comparisons. The same Ontario study also notes that recruitment limitations and selection bias may underlie observed differences [N5-F3]. This is important because if Indigenous peoples are overrepresented in HIV data but not in general population samples, then comparisons can be skewed unless the sampling method explicitly accounts for Indigenous overrepresentation.

Measurement bias can distort comparisons in several ways. The Indigenous review literature emphasizes that structural and social determinants—including colonialism and racism—shape HIV-related behaviors and outcomes [N1-F1]. The stigma and discrimination literature explains that mistrust of healthcare, medical providers, and public health services is a major barrier to prevention, care, and treatment adherence [N3-F2][N3-R4]. If Indigenous peoples are more likely to avoid testing, screening, or reporting, then data on risk behaviors, diagnoses, and outcomes may be missing or biased. The Ontario study also notes that perceived racism, cultural differences, and a shortage of Aboriginal physicians can contribute to barriers to care [N5-F3]. These factors may lead to underreporting of HIV risk behaviors, delayed diagnosis, and underrepresentation in health services, which can make it appear as though Indigenous peoples have different behavioral or social patterns when the true issue is access and reporting bias.

The evidence also suggests that measurement bias can affect the interpretation of behavioral and social findings. The Indigenous review literature states that many of the factors associated with HIV risk also contribute to mistrust of health services, which in turn contributes to poor HIV and health outcomes among Indigenous peoples [N1-F1]. This means that social disadvantages such as poverty, education, employment, and housing are not independent of HIV outcomes; they are part of a causal pathway that also shapes behavior and care engagement [N1-F1][N5-F3]. If studies do not disentangle these pathways, comparisons can confuse social disadvantage with behavior itself. For example, higher rates of injection drug use or inconsistent condom use may reflect both structural disadvantage and actual risk behavior, but without careful control for socioeconomic and geographic barriers, it is difficult to know which effect is dominant [N1-F1][N1-R1][N1-R5].

What evidence is stronger and why? The strongest evidence is generally from studies that explicitly address Indigenous populations and use cohort or longitudinal designs. The Ontario cohort study on late HIV diagnosis is a good example: it compares proportions of late diagnosis between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people within the same cohort and uses logistic regression to assess associations while adjusting for age and HIV risk factor [N5-F3]. This design is stronger than cross-sectional or convenience-sample comparisons because it can better account for time-related changes and confounding variables. The Indigenous HIV review literature is also strong because it synthesizes evidence from four countries and explicitly links HIV-related behaviors to social determinants such as domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use [N1-F1]. This kind of broad, cross-country synthesis is useful for identifying common patterns, but it is less strong for making fine-grained cross-population comparisons than a well-controlled cohort study.

Another strength is the use of direct Indigenous-focused sampling methods. The Ontario study notes that respondent-driven sampling is an effective tool for measuring the health of urban Indigenous communities in Canada [N5-R3]. This is important because it acknowledges that Indigenous populations may require sampling methods that are culturally appropriate and responsive to recruitment barriers. In contrast, general population surveys may miss Indigenous peoples or capture them in ways that do not reflect their true health status. This makes Indigenous-specific sampling methods more valid for comparing Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations when the goal is to assess behavior, access, and outcomes.

In summary, cross-population comparisons are shaped by structural and methodological differences. Indigenous populations are often overrepresented in HIV data but underrepresented in general population samples, which can distort comparisons [N1-F1][N5-F3]. Measurement bias can arise from mistrust, cultural barriers, and underreporting, making behavioral and social findings less reliable [N3-F2][N5-F3]. The strongest evidence comes from cohort studies, Indigenous-focused sampling, and cross-country syntheses that explicitly account for social determinants [N1-F1][N5-F3]. These methodological features matter because they determine whether comparisons are meaningful or merely artifacts of sampling and measurement.

HIV care access and outcomes by Indigenous status show that Indigenous peoples often experience late diagnosis or delayed care, but the evidence also indicates that treatment outcomes can be comparable when care is adequate. The implications for interpreting behavioral and social findings are clear: poor care access and late diagnosis are not simply consequences of risk behaviors; they are part of a larger system of disadvantage that affects both risk and care engagement.

Late diagnosis or delayed care is the strongest documented issue. The Ontario cohort study explicitly states that Aboriginal peoples may receive poorer quality of care once an HIV diagnosis is established and that the study investigated differences in late HIV diagnosis between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people [N5-R1][N6-R1]. It also reports that Aboriginal peoples are more likely to be female, have lower income, education, and employment, and that there is a significant association between Aboriginal ethnicity and late HIV diagnosis defined by CD4+ count after adjusting for age and HIV risk factor [N5-F3]. The study further notes that APHAs were more likely to have a CD4+ count <200 cells/mL at diagnosis, even though clinical outcomes were similar when defined by AIDS-defining illness [N5-F3]. This distinction is important: late diagnosis can be a marker of care quality and access, not just a reflection of behavior alone.

Treatment outcomes and care engagement differences are mixed. The same Ontario study reports that APHAs were more likely to have a CD4+ count <200 cells/mL at diagnosis, but similar clinical outcomes were observed when defined by ADI [N5-F3]. It also notes that additional work is needed to address the socioeconomic and health care needs of APHAs [N5-F3]. The broader evidence from the Indigenous review literature suggests that many factors associated with HIV risk also contribute to mistrust of health services, which in turn contributes to poor HIV and health outcomes among Indigenous peoples [N1-F1]. This means that care engagement differences may be explained partly by distrust, geographic barriers, and structural disadvantage rather than by the presence or absence of risk behaviors alone.

The evidence also supports the idea that care access is constrained by structural factors. The Ontario study notes that limited access to primary health care services among Aboriginal populations in Ontario has been reported based on higher hospital admission rates for conditions that could be managed in ambulatory care settings [N5-F3]. It further states that Aboriginal peoples may experience late diagnosis because of limited access to health care, high concentrations in rural areas, and barriers such as perceived racism, cultural differences, and a shortage of Aboriginal physicians [N5-F3]. These factors help explain why late diagnosis is more common among Indigenous peoples: care access is not only reduced but also delayed by geographic and cultural barriers [N5-F3].

Implications for interpreting behavioral and social findings are therefore significant. Late diagnosis and delayed care should not be read as evidence of higher risk behavior alone. They are also evidence of structural disadvantage, mistrust, and geographic barriers [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F3]. This matters because if a study finds higher rates of injection drug use or inconsistent condom use among Indigenous peoples, those findings must be interpreted in the context of poorer access to prevention and care, not just as evidence of greater individual risk. Similarly, if a study finds lower condom use, that could reflect both behavior and structural barriers to education, health services, and prevention programming [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The Ontario evidence reinforces this point by showing that even when clinical outcomes are comparable, late diagnosis remains a marker of inadequate care and access [N5-F3].

Overall, the evidence shows that Indigenous peoples are more likely to experience late diagnosis or delayed care, but treatment outcomes may still be comparable when care is adequate. The implications are that behavioral and social findings should not be interpreted in isolation from structural and methodological context; care access, stigma, mistrust, and geographic barriers are central to understanding why Indigenous peoples have different HIV trajectories [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F3].

## Integrated synthesis: HIV-related risk behaviors and social disadvantages distinguishing Indigenous peoples from non-Indigenous populations

Indigenous peoples and non-Indigenous populations differ in HIV-related risk behaviors and social disadvantages not because they are fundamentally different in all respects, but because Indigenous peoples are shaped by a distinct set of structural conditions that affect behavior, access to care, and health outcomes. The evidence across the branch reports points to three main themes: **specific HIV-related risk behaviors**, **social and structural disadvantages**, and **the limitations of cross-population comparisons**. These themes are deeply connected because the same social determinants that create poverty, mistrust, and geographic barriers also shape sexual and substance-use risk behaviors and care engagement.

---

## 1. HIV-related risk behaviors: what is documented in Indigenous populations?

The branch reports identify several specific HIV-related risk behaviors in Indigenous populations, with a clear emphasis on **inconsistent and low condom use**, **substance use**, and **high-risk sexual behaviors**.

### Inconsistent and low condom use
The most directly documented Indigenous behavior is inconsistent and low condom use. The Indigenous HIV review literature states that inconsistent and low condom use represents an immediate risk factor for HIV infection and also leads to high rates of STIs in Indigenous populations [N1-R1]. The same source notes that substance use is a determinant of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1], reinforcing the idea that condom use is not isolated from broader risk pathways.

### Substance use
Substance use is another major documented risk behavior. The Indigenous review literature explicitly links substance use to HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that among AI/AN women, reported risk factors for HIV include 54% heterosexual contact and 46% injection drug use [N1-R5]. This means that Indigenous peoples are at risk through both sexual and injection-related pathways. The broader literature also shows that substance use and sexual risk behaviors are associated in adolescents, with substance use linked to ever having sex, multiple sex partners, and other high-risk sexual behaviors [N4-R4]. For Indigenous populations, this association is reinforced by the fact that substance use is tied to injection drug use and other risk factors [N1-F1][N1-R5].

### High-risk sexual behaviors
Sexual behavior is central. The evidence documents heterosexual contact as a reported risk factor among Indigenous women [N1-R5]. The Indigenous review literature also states that domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use are determinants of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1]. This means that sexual risk behaviors in Indigenous populations are not merely individual choices; they are embedded in broader risk environments shaped by structural disadvantage.

### Overlap with non-Indigenous findings
The behaviors overlap with non-Indigenous findings in the sense that condom use, substance use, and sexual risk behaviors are all commonly associated with HIV risk [N1-R1][N1-R5][N4-R4]. But the branch reports also show that they differ in the way they are explained and in the context in which they occur. For Indigenous populations, the evidence points to colonization, racism, social exclusion, and repression of self-determination as the broader determinants [N1-F1]. This means that the same behaviors may be more frequent, more persistent, or more resistant to change because of the structural conditions in which they emerge [N1-F1][N3-F2].

### Role of sexual behavior, substance use, and condom use
These three elements are interrelated. Sexual behavior, particularly heterosexual contact and multiple sexual partners, is documented as a reported risk factor in Indigenous women [N1-R5]. Substance use is a documented determinant of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1], and it is linked to injection drug use and other high-risk pathways [N1-R5]. Condom use is explicitly identified as inconsistent and low, which increases vulnerability to HIV and STIs [N1-R1]. The non-Indigenous literature confirms that substance use and sexual risk behaviors are associated, with condomless sex and peer influence on sex and injecting drug use also being contributing factors [N4-R3][N4-R4]. However, the Indigenous evidence adds that these behaviors are not merely behavioral; they are shaped by social determinants such as poverty, underemployment, poor education, and mistrust of health services [N1-F1][N5-F3].

---

## 2. Social disadvantages distinguishing Indigenous peoples from non-Indigenous populations

Indigenous peoples face a distinct constellation of social disadvantages that are deeply structural, intersectional, and often compounded across multiple life domains. The branch reports show that Indigenous peoples are disadvantaged in **poverty, education, employment, and housing**, and that these disadvantages are shaped by **systemic discrimination and stigma**, which in turn affect health outcomes and access to HIV prevention and care.

### Poverty, education, employment, and housing disadvantages
Poverty is a central disadvantage. The WHO fact sheet notes that Indigenous populations have lower life expectancy than non-Indigenous populations in rich and poor countries alike, and children born in low-income settings face worse outcomes [N2-R1]. The Indigenous HIV review literature states that Indigenous peoples have long-standing connections to their ancestral lands, but colonization, racism, social exclusion, and repression of self-determination have created poverty, underemployment, and poor education [N1-F1]. It also notes that Indigenous peoples in the four study countries have higher poverty rates than non-Indigenous peers, including 28% of Indigenous peoples in the U.S. in 2000 compared to 12% of the total population [N1-F1]. This economic disadvantage is not incidental: it shapes access to food, housing, and basic services, and it is tied to poor HIV outcomes because “many of the factors associated with HIV risk also contribute to mistrust of health services, which in turn contributes to poor HIV and health outcomes among Indigenous peoples” [N1-F1].

Education and employment disadvantages are similarly central. The Indigenous review literature states that subsequent legal, political, and social marginalization was often coupled with racial prejudice to produce poverty, underemployment, and poor education [N1-F1]. The same source also notes that residential schools and “stolen generations” exacerbated displacement and loss of identity and were often associated with physical and sexual abuse that affected future generations [N1-F1]. These historical and ongoing disadvantages are part of why Indigenous populations have poorer health outcomes and are more vulnerable to HIV-related risk pathways.

Housing insecurity and geographic barriers are also a key disadvantage. The Indigenous review literature emphasizes that colonization disrupted traditional lands and cultures, and that this alienation from territory and domination by outsiders adversely affected physical, social, and emotional wellbeing by suppressing traditional life and customs [N1-F1]. Indigenous peoples are often concentrated in rural areas, where access to health care is limited. The Ontario study on late HIV diagnosis notes that Aboriginal peoples may experience late diagnosis because of limited access to health care, high concentrations in rural areas, and barriers such as perceived racism, cultural differences, and a shortage of Aboriginal physicians [N5-F3]. This geographic and cultural distance from services is not only a structural barrier but also a source of mistrust, which further delays care.

### Systemic discrimination and stigma affecting health outcomes
Systemic discrimination and stigma are central to health outcomes. The Indigenous review literature states that Indigenous peoples have been identified as a population group that experiences social and economic determinants—including colonialism and racism—that increase exposure to HIV [N1-F1]. The stigma and discrimination literature adds that a history of unethical medical experimentation and contemporary discrimination within healthcare settings has resulted in mistrust of healthcare, medical providers, medical treatments, and the public health establishment among Black, Latino, and other communities [N3-F2]. This mistrust is described as a major barrier to HIV prevention, care, and treatment adherence, particularly among Indigenous peoples [N3-R4]. The same source also explains that Indigenous people living with HIV face barriers through stigma and discrimination inhibiting access to supports including family, peers, and community resources [N3-R2]. The broader Stigma and HIV Disparities Model shows how societal stigma manifests through residential segregation, historical trauma, and mistrust, and how these structural and individual-level manifestations reinforce differences in status, resources, and social/political influence [N3-F2]. This means that stigma is not a separate factor but a mechanism through which poverty, education, employment, and housing disadvantages shape health outcomes.

### Cultural and geographic barriers to HIV prevention and care
Cultural and geographic barriers are therefore part of a single structural system. The Ontario evidence notes that perceived racism, differences in cultural beliefs and values, and a shortage of Aboriginal physicians contribute to barriers to care [N5-F3]. In the Indigenous review literature, the authors describe how colonialism and racism have produced poverty, underemployment, poor education, and poor health outcomes, and how these conditions also contribute to mistrust of health services [N1-F1]. Together, these sources show that Indigenous peoples do not simply face HIV risk because of individual choices; they face a complex set of disadvantages that include economic deprivation, educational disadvantage, employment barriers, housing insecurity, geographic isolation, and stigma.

---

## 3. Structural and methodological factors shaping cross-population comparisons

Cross-population comparisons between Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations are shaped by important structural and methodological differences, and these differences make comparisons difficult and potentially misleading. The branch reports show that data collection and sampling differ across populations, that measurement bias can distort comparisons, and that the strongest evidence is generally from studies that explicitly address Indigenous populations and use cohort or longitudinal designs.

### Differences in data collection and sampling
Indigenous populations are often overrepresented in HIV data but underrepresented in general population samples. The Indigenous HIV review literature notes that Indigenous peoples are overrepresented in the HIV epidemic in Canada, yet they are underrepresented in research [N1-F1]. The Ontario study on late HIV diagnosis explicitly states that Aboriginal people are over-represented by approximately 4.6 times in the HIV epidemic in Canada, while they represent only 6.0% of the total population [N5-F3]. This overrepresentation indicates that Indigenous populations may not be sampled proportionally in many HIV datasets, which can distort comparisons. The same study also notes that recruitment limitations and selection bias may underlie observed differences [N5-F3]. This is important because if Indigenous peoples are overrepresented in HIV data but not in general population samples, then comparisons can be skewed unless the sampling method explicitly accounts for Indigenous overrepresentation.

### Measurement bias and distorted comparisons
Measurement bias can distort comparisons in several ways. The Indigenous review literature emphasizes that structural and social determinants—including colonialism and racism—shape HIV-related behaviors and outcomes [N1-F1]. The stigma and discrimination literature explains that mistrust of healthcare, medical providers, and public health services is a major barrier to prevention, care, and treatment adherence [N3-F2][N3-R4]. If Indigenous peoples are more likely to avoid testing, screening, or reporting, then data on risk behaviors, diagnoses, and outcomes may be missing or biased. The Ontario study also notes that perceived racism, cultural differences, and a shortage of Aboriginal physicians can contribute to barriers to care [N5-F3]. These factors may lead to underreporting of HIV risk behaviors, delayed diagnosis, and underrepresentation in health services, which can make it appear as though Indigenous peoples have different behavioral or social patterns when the true issue is access and reporting bias.

### What evidence is stronger and why?
The strongest evidence is generally from studies that explicitly address Indigenous populations and use cohort or longitudinal designs. The Ontario cohort study on late HIV diagnosis is a good example: it compares proportions of late diagnosis between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people within the same cohort and uses logistic regression to assess associations while adjusting for age and HIV risk factor [N5-F3]. This design is stronger than cross-sectional or convenience-sample comparisons because it can better account for time-related changes and confounding variables. The Indigenous HIV review literature is also strong because it synthesizes evidence from four countries and explicitly links HIV-related behaviors to social determinants such as domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use [N1-F1]. This kind of broad, cross-country synthesis is useful for identifying common patterns, but it is less strong for making fine-grained cross-population comparisons than a well-controlled cohort study.

Another strength is the use of direct Indigenous-focused sampling methods. The Ontario study notes that respondent-driven sampling is an effective tool for measuring the health of urban Indigenous communities in Canada [N5-R3]. This is important because it acknowledges that Indigenous populations may require sampling methods that are culturally appropriate and responsive to recruitment barriers. In contrast, general population surveys may miss Indigenous peoples or capture them in ways that do not reflect their true health status. This makes Indigenous-specific sampling methods more valid for comparing Indigenous and non-Indigenous populations when the goal is to assess behavior, access, and outcomes.

---

## 4. HIV care access and outcomes by Indigenous status

HIV care access and outcomes by Indigenous status show that Indigenous peoples often experience **late diagnosis or delayed care**, but the evidence also indicates that **treatment outcomes can be comparable when care is adequate**. The implications for interpreting behavioral and social findings are significant: poor care access and late diagnosis are not simply consequences of risk behaviors; they are part of a larger system of disadvantage that affects both risk and care engagement.

### Late diagnosis or delayed care
Late diagnosis or delayed care is the strongest documented issue. The Ontario cohort study explicitly states that Aboriginal peoples may receive poorer quality of care once an HIV diagnosis is established and that the study investigated differences in late HIV diagnosis between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people [N5-R1][N6-R1]. It also reports that Aboriginal peoples are more likely to be female, have lower income, education, and employment, and that there is a significant association between Aboriginal ethnicity and late HIV diagnosis defined by CD4+ count after adjusting for age and HIV risk factor [N5-F3]. The study further notes that APHAs were more likely to have a CD4+ count <200 cells/mL at diagnosis, even though clinical outcomes were similar when defined by AIDS-defining illness [N5-F3]. This distinction is important: late diagnosis can be a marker of care quality and access, not just a reflection of behavior alone.

### Treatment outcomes and care engagement differences
The evidence also supports the idea that care access is constrained by structural factors. The Ontario study notes that limited access to primary health care services among Aboriginal populations in Ontario has been reported based on higher hospital admission rates for conditions that could be managed in ambulatory care settings [N5-F3]. It further states that Aboriginal peoples may experience late diagnosis because of limited access to health care, high concentrations in rural areas, and barriers such as perceived racism, cultural differences, and a shortage of Aboriginal physicians [N5-F3]. These factors help explain why late diagnosis is more common among Indigenous peoples: care access is not only reduced but also delayed by geographic and cultural barriers [N5-F3].

### Implications for interpreting behavioral and social findings
The implications are clear: late diagnosis and delayed care should not be read as evidence of higher risk behavior alone. They are also evidence of structural disadvantage, mistrust, and geographic barriers [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-F3]. This matters because if a study finds higher rates of injection drug use or inconsistent condom use among Indigenous peoples, those findings must be interpreted in the context of poorer access to prevention and care, not just as evidence of greater individual risk. Similarly, if a study finds lower condom use, that could reflect both behavior and structural barriers to education, health services, and prevention programming [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The Ontario evidence reinforces this point by showing that even when clinical outcomes are comparable, late diagnosis remains a marker of inadequate care and access [N5-F3].

---

## 5. Integrated conclusion

Overall, Indigenous peoples and non-Indigenous populations differ in HIV-related risk behaviors and social disadvantages because Indigenous peoples are shaped by a distinct set of structural conditions that affect behavior, access to care, and health outcomes. The evidence shows that Indigenous peoples face:

- **Specific HIV-related risk behaviors** such as inconsistent and low condom use, substance use, and high-risk sexual behaviors [N1-R1][N1-R5][N4-R4].
- **Social and structural disadvantages** including poverty, education, employment, and housing insecurity, as well as systemic discrimination, stigma, and cultural/ geographic barriers to HIV prevention and care [N2-R1][N1-F1][N5-F3][N3-F2].
- **Cross-population comparisons** that are difficult because of differences in data collection, sampling, and measurement bias, with the strongest evidence coming from Indigenous-focused cohort studies and synthesis of social determinants [N1-F1][N5-F3][N5-R3].
- **HIV care access and outcomes** that often show late diagnosis or delayed care, but also comparable treatment outcomes when care is adequate [N5-F3][N5-R1][N6-R1].

In short, Indigenous peoples are not simply a population with a different set of risk behaviors; they are a population shaped by colonization, racism, poverty, mistrust, and geographic isolation. These conditions create a distinct social and structural context that distinguishes them from non-Indigenous populations and must be taken into account when interpreting behavioral, social, and health outcomes.

The HIV-related risk behaviors documented in Indigenous populations include inconsistent and low condom use, substance use, and high-risk sexual behaviors associated with injection drug use and other risk factors. These behaviors are not unique to Indigenous peoples, but the evidence suggests that they appear in Indigenous populations within a specific social context shaped by colonization, marginalization, and structural disadvantage, and that their expression may differ in ways that overlap with and diverge from non-Indigenous findings.

Specific risk behaviors documented in Indigenous populations are most clearly condom-related and substance-related. The Indigenous HIV review literature states that inconsistent and low condom use represents an immediate risk factor for HIV infection, which also leads to high rates of STIs in Indigenous populations [N1-R1]. It also notes that among AI/AN women, reported risk factors for HIV include 54% heterosexual contact and 46% injection drug use [N1-R5]. This indicates that Indigenous peoples are at risk through both sexual and injection-related pathways. The broader review literature also highlights that domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use are determinants of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1].

Sexual behavior is central. The evidence explicitly identifies heterosexual contact as a reported risk factor among Indigenous women [N1-R5]. The Indigenous review literature also notes that HIV-related behaviors are shaped by social determinants including domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use [N1-F1]. This means that sexual risk behaviors in Indigenous populations are not simply about individual choice; they are embedded in broader risk environments.

Substance use is another major documented risk behavior. The Indigenous review literature explicitly states that substance use is a determinant of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1]. The American Indian/Alaska Native youth study on substance use and sexual risk behaviors notes that the prevalence of behaviors putting AI/AN high school students at risk for teen pregnancy and STIs was examined [N1-R2]. The CDC-linked excerpt also states that studies among adolescents show an association between substance use and sexual risk behaviors, including ever having sex, having multiple sex partners, and other high-risk sexual behaviors [N4-R4]. For Indigenous populations, this association is reinforced by the fact that substance use is tied to injection drug use and other risk factors [N1-F1][N1-R5]. The evidence also notes that IV drug use is recognized as a risk factor in Native communities [N1-R4].

Condom use is explicitly documented as inconsistent and low in Indigenous populations. The Indigenous review literature states that inconsistent and low condom use is an immediate risk factor for HIV infection and contributes to high STI rates [N1-R1]. The non-Indigenous literature in the search set supports the general association between substance use and sexual risk behaviors, including condomless sex and other behaviors linked to STI testing [N4-R2]. However, the Indigenous evidence shows that these behaviors appear within a context of colonization, racism, social exclusion, and repression of self-determination [N1-F1], which means that the same sexual and substance-use risk patterns may be expressed differently because of structural disadvantage rather than being identical to non-Indigenous patterns.

The role of sexual behavior, substance use, and condom use is therefore interrelated. Sexual behavior, particularly heterosexual contact and multiple sexual partners, is documented as a reported risk factor in Indigenous women [N1-R5]. Substance use is a documented determinant of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1], and it is linked to injection drug use and other high-risk pathways [N1-R5]. Condom use is explicitly identified as inconsistent and low, which increases vulnerability to HIV and STIs [N1-R1]. The non-Indigenous literature confirms that substance use and sexual risk behaviors are associated, with condomless sex and peer influence on sex and injecting drug use also being contributing factors [N4-R3][N4-R4]. However, the Indigenous evidence adds that these behaviors are not merely behavioral; they are shaped by social determinants such as poverty, underemployment, poor education, and mistrust of health services [N1-F1][N5-F3].

In terms of overlap and difference, the behaviors overlap with non-Indigenous findings in the sense that condom use, substance use, and sexual risk behaviors are all commonly associated with HIV risk [N1-R1][N1-R5][N4-R4]. But they differ in the way they are explained and in the context in which they occur. ---

## 1. HIV-related risk behaviors: what is documented in Indigenous populations?

The branch reports identify several specific HIV-related risk behaviors in Indigenous populations, with a clear emphasis on **inconsistent and low condom use**, **substance use**, and **high-risk sexual behaviors**.

### Inconsistent and low condom use
The most directly documented Indigenous behavior is inconsistent and low condom use. The Indigenous HIV review literature states that inconsistent and low condom use represents an immediate risk factor for HIV infection and also leads to high rates of STIs in Indigenous populations [N1-R1]. The same source notes that substance use is a determinant of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1], reinforcing the idea that condom use is not isolated from broader risk pathways.

### Substance use
Substance use is another major documented risk behavior. The Indigenous review literature explicitly links substance use to HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that among AI/AN women, reported risk factors for HIV include 54% heterosexual contact and 46% injection drug use [N1-R5]. This means that Indigenous peoples are at risk through both sexual and injection-related pathways. The broader literature also shows that substance use and sexual risk behaviors are associated in adolescents, with substance use linked to ever having sex, multiple sex partners, and other high-risk sexual behaviors [N4-R4]. For Indigenous populations, this association is reinforced by the fact that substance use is tied to injection drug use and other risk factors [N1-F1][N1-R5].

### High-risk sexual behaviors
Sexual behavior is central. The evidence documents heterosexual contact as a reported risk factor among Indigenous women [N1-R5]. The Indigenous review literature also states that domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use are determinants of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1]. This means that sexual risk behaviors in Indigenous populations are not merely individual choices; they are embedded in broader risk environments shaped by structural disadvantage.

### Overlap with non-Indigenous findings
The behaviors overlap with non-Indigenous findings in the sense that condom use, substance use, and sexual risk behaviors are all commonly associated with HIV risk [N1-R1][N1-R5][N4-R4]. But the branch reports also show that they differ in the way they are explained and in the context in which they occur. For Indigenous populations, the evidence points to colonization, racism, social exclusion, and repression of self-determination as the broader determinants [N1-F1]. This means that the same behaviors may be more frequent, more persistent, or more resistant to change because of the structural conditions in which they emerge [N1-F1][N3-F2].

### Role of sexual behavior, substance use, and condom use
These three elements are interrelated. Sexual behavior, particularly heterosexual contact and multiple sexual partners, is documented as a reported risk factor in Indigenous women [N1-R5]. Substance use is a documented determinant of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1], and it is linked to injection drug use and other high-risk pathways [N1-R5]. Condom use is explicitly identified as inconsistent and low, which increases vulnerability to HIV and STIs [N1-R1]. The non-Indigenous literature confirms that substance use and sexual risk behaviors are associated, with condomless sex and peer influence on sex and injecting drug use also being contributing factors [N4-R3][N4-R4]. ---

## 2. Social disadvantages distinguishing Indigenous peoples from non-Indigenous populations

The HIV-related risk behaviors documented in Indigenous populations include inconsistent and low condom use, substance use, and high-risk sexual behaviors associated with injection drug use and other risk factors. These behaviors are not unique to Indigenous peoples, but the evidence suggests that they appear in Indigenous populations within a specific social context shaped by colonization, marginalization, and structural disadvantage, and that their expression may differ in ways that overlap with and diverge from non-Indigenous findings.

Specific risk behaviors documented in Indigenous populations are most clearly condom-related and substance-related. The Indigenous HIV review literature states that inconsistent and low condom use represents an immediate risk factor for HIV infection, which also leads to high rates of STIs in Indigenous populations [N1-R1]. It also notes that among AI/AN women, reported risk factors for HIV include 54% heterosexual contact and 46% injection drug use [N1-R5]. This indicates that Indigenous peoples are at risk through both sexual and injection-related pathways. The broader review literature also highlights that domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use are determinants of HIV-related behaviors [N1-F1].

The Indigenous review literature also notes that HIV-related behaviors are shaped by social determinants including domestic violence, stigma and discrimination, and injecting drug use [N1-F1]. This means that sexual risk behaviors in Indigenous populations are not simply about individual choice; they are embedded in broader risk environments.

The American Indian/Alaska Native youth study on substance use and sexual risk behaviors notes that the prevalence of behaviors putting AI/AN high school students at risk for teen pregnancy and STIs was examined [N1-R2]. The CDC-linked excerpt also states that studies among adolescents show an association between substance use and sexual risk behaviors, including ever having sex, having multiple sex partners, and other high-risk sexual behaviors [N4-R4]. For Indigenous populations, this association is reinforced by the fact that substance use is tied to injection drug use and other risk factors [N1-F1][N1-R5].
